title: The deepest hole
teaches: Project Mohole, the Kola Superdeep Borehole and KTB: what drilling into the crust found, and why the holes stopped

parts.title: A drill ship with no anchor

blocks.text: Everything in this branch so far was learned at a distance, from gravity and from waves. In 1957 a group of American scientists, including Walter Munk, an oceanographer known for his work on waves and tides, and the geologist Harry Hess of lesson 9, asked why no one had simply drilled through the crust and brought back a piece of the mantle. Their informal club, the American Miscellaneous Society, proposed **Project Mohole**: a hole to the Moho.

They chose the ocean. Lesson D3 showed that ocean crust is only about 7 kilometres thick, against 30 to 50 under the continents. The difficulty was that the sea floor there is several kilometres under water. In March and April 1961 a converted oil-drilling barge, CUSS I, drilled at a site in water 3,560 metres deep off Guadalupe Island, Mexico. No anchor could reach the bottom. Instead four large engines with propellers, mounted on the hull and able to push it in any direction, were steered by a crew who watched sonar and radar markers around the site and nudged the barge back whenever it drifted. Holding a ship in place this way, now called dynamic positioning, is standard in offshore drilling. The drill went 183 metres into the sea floor and its last few metres were basalt, the first sample ever drilled from the second layer of the ocean crust beneath the sediments. The novelist John Steinbeck was aboard to write about it for *Life* magazine.

That was as deep as Mohole went. The next phase was to drill all the way through the ocean crust, several kilometres of hard rock, which needed a much larger purpose-built ship. Its estimated cost multiplied, the project became mired in disputes over contractors, and in 1966 Congress refused further money for it. But its methods survived: the Deep Sea Drilling Project's ship *Glomar Challenger* began work in 1968 and drilled hundreds of holes across the oceans, recovering the sediments that confirmed the sea floor gets older away from the ridges (lesson 9).

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Project Mohole (proposed 1957) aimed to drill through the thin ocean crust to the Moho.
In 1961 CUSS I drilled 183 m into the sea floor in 3,560 m of water, holding position without anchors, and recovered basalt.
Mohole was cancelled in 1966, but its methods led to the scientific ocean drilling that confirmed seafloor spreading.

blocks.text: The Soviet Union chose a different route: drill on land, where the work is easier, and go as deep as possible. On 24 May 1970, on the Kola Peninsula in the far northwest of Russia, near the Norwegian border, drilling began on a hole designated SG-3. The site sits on the Baltic Shield, a region of very old, hard crystalline rock, some of it more than 2.5 billion years old. The goal was 15 kilometres.

Drilling that deep needs a new approach. Normally a drill bit is turned by spinning the whole string of pipe from the surface, but a string 12 kilometres long would twist itself apart. The Kola team rotated the pipe slowly and did most of the work with a turbine at the bottom, powered by **drilling mud**, a heavy fluid pumped down the pipe that also cools the bit, carries the rock chips back up, and presses on the walls to keep the hole open. Much of the pipe was made of aluminium alloy, lighter than steel, so that the string would not tear itself apart under its own weight. Each time the bit wore out, which in deep hard rock was every few hours of drilling, the whole string had to be pulled up, unscrewed in sections and lowered again, which took many hours. The lower hole was 21.5 centimetres across. In 1989 it reached 12,262 metres, the deepest hole ever drilled, a record it still holds.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: The Kola Superdeep Borehole (SG-3) began in 1970 in ancient rock of the Baltic Shield, aiming for 15 km.
It drove the bit with a turbine at the bottom of the hole rather than spinning the whole pipe at full speed.
It reached 12,262 m in 1989, still the deepest hole ever drilled.

blocks.text: Kola was drilled partly to test what seismology said. Surveys of the kind in lesson D3 showed a boundary in the continental crust there, about 7 kilometres down, where wave speeds increased. Boundaries like this, within the crust and well above the Moho, had been named the Conrad discontinuity, and the textbook interpretation was that granite-like rock gave way to basalt-like rock there. Below nearly 7 kilometres the drill passed instead out of volcanic and sedimentary rocks into granite-like gneiss (a banded metamorphic rock, lesson 5). The seismic boundary was a metamorphic transition and the top of a zone where the rock was cracked and filled with water. The lesson for geologists was that a change in wave speed marks a change in rock properties, which is not necessarily the change in rock type they had predicted.

That water was the second surprise. The rock at several kilometres down was expected to be dry and tight. Instead it was fractured and wet, with water that had been squeezed out of minerals during metamorphism and trapped beneath impermeable rock above. The drilling mud came back up bubbling with hydrogen, helium, methane and other gases. And in cores from between 6 and 7 kilometres down, Soviet scientists reported microscopic fossils of 24 species of single-celled organisms preserved as carbon-rich remains; some scientists have questioned whether they could have been contamination from the drilling mud.

The third surprise stopped the project. Temperatures had been predicted to reach about 100 °C at 10 kilometres. At 12 kilometres the rock was about 180 °C. At that temperature, and under that pressure, the rock was weaker and behaved more like a stiff plastic than a brittle solid; the walls of the hole crept inward, and every time the bit was pulled out, the hole began to close. Equipment failed faster in the heat. After several attempts to push deeper ended in lost and stuck pipe, drilling stopped in 1992. With the end of the Soviet Union money ran short, the site was kept for measurements for some years, and it was finally closed down in the mid-2000s. The opening is now sealed with a bolted metal cap.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: At about 7 km Kola found no basalt layer where the seismic boundary had been read as one; the boundary was a metamorphic zone of cracked rock full of water.
It found water and gases deep in the crust, and reported microfossils from between 6 and 7 km.
The rock at 12 km was about 180 °C instead of the ~100 °C expected from early predictions, and the hot rock crept into the hole.

blocks.text: Every deep hole meets the same limit. Rock gets hotter with depth, by about 25 °C per kilometre on average in continental crust (lesson 7's gradient from Kelvin's mines), and less in old, cold crust: at Kola about 14 °C per kilometre on average. Drill bits, pipe, the mud and the instruments all have temperature limits, and hot rock under great pressure creeps into the hole. So how quickly the rock warms with depth largely decides how deep a hole can go.

The German Continental Deep Drilling Program, KTB, tested this in Bavaria. A pilot hole reached 4,000 metres in 1989, and the main hole began in 1990 at Windischeschenbach, with an initial goal of 10 kilometres. The rock there warmed by nearly 28 °C per kilometre, almost twice Kola's average rate, and its equipment could not work for long above about 265 °C. How deep could it go?

blocks.caption: Temperature against depth, for rock warming at the rate you set from a surface at 10 °C. The hole stops where the rock is hotter than the drill can stand. The real holes are marked; Kola's predicted temperature is the dotted line.
blocks.task: Set KTB’s warming, about 28 °C per km, and its limit of 265 °C

blocks.text: In 1994, at 9,101 metres, the rock at the bottom was 265 °C and KTB was stopped: in rock that warms faster, the same limit comes much sooner, and the hole ended 3 kilometres shallower than Kola.

blocks.caption: The deepest hole against other depths, and Everest's height, on a scale where each mark is ten times the last.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Rock warms with depth, about 25 °C per km on average under continents.
Heat limits drilling: equipment fails and hot rock creeps into the hole. KTB's rock warmed nearly twice as fast as Kola's, and it stopped shallower.
KTB in Germany, in rock warming nearly 28 °C per km, stopped at 9,101 m and 265 °C in 1994.

blocks.text: The deepest hole on Earth reached about a third of the way to the Moho beneath it, which lies about 40 kilometres down, and about one five-hundredth of the way to the centre. Holes for oil and gas have since been drilled longer than Kola, more than 12 kilometres measured along the pipe, but they curve over and run sideways through the oil-bearing rock, so their vertical depth is much less.

The Mohole idea survives in the ocean. The drilling ship *JOIDES Resolution*, a successor to *Glomar Challenger*, drilled for nearly four decades, and Japan's larger ship *Chikyu*, built partly with the aim of reaching the mantle, has drilled into the sea floor since 2005. The deepest hole into intact ocean crust, Hole 504B in the eastern Pacific south of Costa Rica, reached about 2.1 kilometres below the sea floor, still kilometres short of the Moho. In 2023 *JOIDES Resolution* took a different approach: on the Atlantis Massif in the mid-Atlantic, where a fault has brought mantle rock up to the sea floor, it drilled 1,268 metres into mantle peridotite (the olivine-rich rock of lesson D3) and brought up the longest core of mantle rock yet.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Kola went about a third of the way to the Moho under it.
Ocean drilling has not yet crossed the Moho; the deepest hole into ocean crust is about 2.1 km.
In 2023 a ship drilled 1,268 m into mantle rock exposed on the Atlantic sea floor by faulting.

blocks.caption: Six questions on deep drilling
blocks.task: Select the best answer for each question

items.ask: Why did Project Mohole plan to drill in the ocean rather than on land?
choices: Ocean crust is only about 7 km thick, so the Moho is much nearer
Ocean rock is softer and easier to drill
Drilling on land was banned by treaty
items.why: Under continents the Moho is 30 to 50 km down; under the oceans it is about 7 km below the sea floor.

items.ask: What did Kola find at about 7 km, where seismologists had expected granite-like rock to give way to a basalt layer?
choices: Granite-like gneiss, cracked, altered and full of water
A layer of basalt, as predicted
items.why: The seismic boundary marked a change in the rock's physical state and metamorphism, including fractured rock filled with fluid, rather than a basalt layer.

items.ask: Why did drilling at Kola stop short of its 15 km goal?
choices: The rock was about 180 °C, much hotter than predicted, so it crept into the hole and pipe was lost and stuck
items.why: At high temperature and pressure the rock behaved plastically and the hole kept closing, while equipment failed faster in the heat.

items.ask: KTB's rock warmed almost twice as fast with depth as Kola's. What did that mean for how deep it could go?
choices: It reached the drill's temperature limit sooner, and stopped at 9.1 km
It could go deeper, because hot rock is softer to drill
items.why: A steeper temperature gradient reaches any fixed limit at a shallower depth.

items.ask: How did CUSS I stay above its hole in water 3,560 m deep?
choices: Outboard motors, steered by crew watching sonar and radar markers, held it in place
It was tied to an oil platform
items.why: No anchor could reach the bottom. Holding position with steered propellers, now called dynamic positioning, was first done on Mohole.

items.ask: What was unusual about the 2023 Atlantis Massif hole?
choices: It brought up the longest core of mantle rock yet, 1,268 m, where a fault had brought the mantle near the sea floor
It was the first hole to cross the Moho
It was drilled from the Moon
items.why: The drill did not cross the Moho. A fault had brought mantle peridotite to the sea floor, so the drill could sample it directly.

learned: Project Mohole (1961) drilled 183 m into the sea floor from a drill ship held in place without anchors, and was cancelled in 1966.
The Kola Superdeep Borehole reached 12,262 m in 1989, finding unexpected water, no deep basalt layer, and rock at 180 °C.
Heat sets the limit: KTB stopped at 9,101 m and 265 °C.
No hole has reached the Moho; mantle rock has been drilled where faults bring it near the sea floor.
